summary: This lead seal of Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria carries on one face a frontal bust of Christ Pantokrator, his head set against a cross-nimbus and framed by a circular inscription, and on the other a bust of the Theotokos. Pressed onto the cords that closed a document, it placed the ruler's correspondence under the protection of Christ and his Mother. It shows how quickly the Byzantine image of Christ became part of the visual language of power among the newly Christian Slavs.
facts: The Commons record identifies the type as Iordanov Type III.2.A, the reference classification of Bulgarian medieval seals by Ivan Iordanov.
Simeon I (reigned 893–927), educated in Constantinople, presided over a flowering of Old Church Slavonic letters and claimed the imperial title of tsar.
Like Byzantine imperial seals, Bulgarian royal seals were struck in lead with a bulloterion (a pincer-like matrix) on cords attached to documents.
notes: The photographed specimen is a numismatic-trade piece (CNG); its present owner is not recorded. One entry stands for the seal type.

summary: On the obverse of this small lead seal Christ appears as Pantokrator, a frontal half-length bust with cross-nimbus; on the reverse Tsar Peter I of Bulgaria and his Byzantine wife Irene (Maria) Lekapene stand side by side, holding a patriarchal cross between them. The arrangement copies the imperial seals and coins of Constantinople, where Christ occupies the place of honour above the rulers who govern in his name.
facts: Irene (Maria) Lekapene was a granddaughter of Emperor Romanos I Lekapenos; her marriage to Peter in 927 sealed peace between Byzantium and Bulgaria.
The design of a ruling couple holding a cross between them follows contemporary Byzantine imperial iconography.
notes: Numismatic-trade specimen photographed by CNG; one entry stands for the seal type.

summary: The seal of Photios, the learned Patriarch of Constantinople, shows the Theotokos Hodegetria standing frontally and holding the Christ Child on her left arm, with the invocation 'Most Holy Hodegetria'; the reverse names Photios as archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, in five lines. Made in the first generation after the end of Iconoclasm, it testifies to the restored place of the image of the incarnate Christ in the life of the Church.
facts: Photios served twice as patriarch (858–867 and 877–886) and was one of the most learned men of the Byzantine Middle Ages.
The Hodegetria ('She who shows the Way') was the name of a celebrated icon of the Virgin pointing to the Child, kept in Constantinople.
The Commons description cites the standard corpus BLS II 7a (Zacos–Veglery/Seibt) for the type.
notes: The Commons file name calls this a 'coin', but its description identifies it correctly as a lead seal (PB seal). Numismatic-trade specimen; a closely similar seal of Patriarch Stephen (886–893 or 925–928) also exists on Commons.

summary: The Theotokos stands frontally in chiton and maphorion, holding on her left arm the Christ Child, who wears tunic and mantle and holds a scroll; cruciform invocation monograms flank the figure. The reverse gives the name of Symeon, metropolitan of Seleucia. Struck around 800, in the very decades of the iconoclast controversy, the seal shows a bishop who chose the image of the incarnate Christ with his Mother as his personal emblem.
facts: The Commons record dates the seal to Symeon's tenure, c. 787–815, beginning in the year of the Second Council of Nicaea, which restored the veneration of icons.
Seleucia (modern Silifke in southern Turkey) was the metropolitan see of the province of Isauria.
notes: Numismatic-trade specimen photographed by CNG.

summary: On this seal the Theotokos appears as a frontal bust holding before her breast a medallion containing the bust of the Christ Child, flanked by cruciform monograms; the reverse invokes her help for 'your servant Paul, metropolitan of Seleucia'. The image of Christ shown within a clipeus held by his Mother is an early form of the type later called the Virgin Nikopoios or Blachernitissa.
facts: The circular legend on the reverse reads, in Greek, 'Theotokos, help your servant', a formula found on countless Byzantine seals.
Seals of this kind were attached by cords to letters and documents to authenticate them and keep them closed.
notes: Numismatic-trade specimen photographed by CNG; the iconographic label 'Nikopoios/Blachernitissa' is a later art-historical term.

summary: This fragile linen hanging, its blue resist-dyed pattern now worn and fragmentary, once told biblical stories in registers. According to the museum, the upper register shows the Virgin with the Christ Child on a cross-legged stool while the Magi approach with gifts, identified by a Coptic inscription; the middle register may show the Baptism of Christ and the Multiplication of the Loaves and Fishes, and below Jonah is swallowed by the sea monster. Such hangings brought the Gospel into the homes and churches of Christian Egypt.
facts: The cloth was decorated by resist-dyeing: areas protected by a paste or wax stayed undyed when the fabric was dipped in indigo, leaving the figures in light outline.
The museum notes that a Coptic inscription identifies the three kings approaching the Virgin and Child.
notes: The museum itself marks the Baptism identification as uncertain ('may depict').

summary: A large, faded linen from Akhmim in Upper Egypt carries several biblical scenes in dyed outline, separated by bands of discs and blossoms. The museum identifies Moses receiving the Law and, in the lower left, the woman with the issue of blood reaching out to touch the robe of Christ. Though the figures are now hard to read, the cloth is a rare early example of Gospel miracles depicted on a domestic textile.
facts: Akhmim (ancient Panopolis) was one of the great sources of late Roman and Coptic textiles preserved in Egyptian burials.
The V&A acquired the piece in 1897 (museum number 722-1897).
notes: Christ's figure is very faint in the photograph; identification rests on the museum's description.

summary: This narrow fragment of brightly coloured slit tapestry, woven in yellow, black, blue and white on a red ground, shows two richly dressed figures beneath a Coptic inscription and, below, Joseph and Mary holding the infant Jesus, apparently seated on a horse or donkey. The scene may evoke the Holy Family's journey, and the strong outlines and large eyes are typical of Coptic weaving of the early Islamic centuries.
facts: The fragment is only 18.5 cm high; one edge preserves the original selvedge.
Coptic inscriptions accompany both scenes, a sign of the growing use of the Coptic language in Egyptian church art.
notes: The V&A says the figures 'may be sitting on a horse'; reading the scene as the Flight into Egypt is therefore tentative, and the scripture reference is given only as a possibility.

summary: Woven in red, yellow, blue and black, this roundel shows the Virgin enthroned frontally with the Christ Child, while the Magi, reduced to bold geometric shapes with large staring eyes, crowd in from the side to offer their gifts. The abstraction of the figures is characteristic of later Coptic tapestry, in which a familiar Gospel scene became almost an emblem.
facts: The museum's label dates the textile to the 7th–8th century and identifies it as wool and linen from Coptic Egypt.
Roundels (orbiculi) like this were sewn onto tunics or furnishing fabrics.

summary: On this ragged fragment of pale cloth a row of figures is drawn in fine dark outline: a haloed figure, labelled by the museum as Christ, among a group of disciples, one of whom raises an arm. The museum's title associates the scene with Christ and his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. Even in its damaged state it preserves the delicate linear drawing of Coptic artists of the 6th century.
facts: The Florence archaeological museum holds one of Italy's principal collections of Coptic textiles, formed largely in the 19th century.
notes: Title and date are taken from the museum label as transcribed by the photographer; the exact technique (drawn or painted outline on linen) is not stated in the available record, and the scene identification cannot be checked from the image alone.

summary: Beneath a pierced arch with a beaded border, the Virgin lies on her bier surrounded by grieving apostles who bend over her head and feet. Behind the bier stands Christ, who holds his Mother's soul, shown as a small swaddled child, while angels descend with veiled hands to receive it. The ivory's crisp carving, deep undercutting and architectural frame are characteristic of the finest Constantinopolitan work of the late 10th century.
facts: The scene of the Koimesis reverses the familiar image of the Virgin holding the infant Christ: here Christ holds his Mother's soul as she once held him.
The plaque came to the Met as part of the J. Pierpont Morgan gift of 1917.

summary: The Virgin lies on her deathbed among the mourning apostles, while Christ stands behind the bier and receives her swaddled, child-like soul; two angels descend with veiled hands to carry it to heaven. As the museum notes, Saint Peter swings a censer at the left and Saint Paul, at the right, bends to kiss the Virgin's feet.
facts: The Greek name of the feast, Koimesis, means 'falling asleep'.
Before entering the Walters collection in 1927 the plaque passed through the hands of the Berlin dealer Paul Cassirer and the Paris dealer Henri Daguerre.

summary: Carved from a section of elephant tusk, this cylindrical box is wrapped with New Testament scenes: according to the museum, the Annunciation, Christ's entry into Jerusalem, the Raising of Lazarus and the Healing of the Blind Man, together with an altar bearing chalices. The altar scene suggests that the pyx served in the liturgy, perhaps to hold the consecrated bread or relics, surrounding the Eucharist with images of Christ's life-giving power.
facts: The Greek word pyxis originally meant a box made of boxwood; the name passed to round ivory boxes of this type.
Pyxides were made from cross-sections of elephant tusk, which explains their cylindrical form.

summary: At the heart of this jewelled reliquary, shaped like a precious book cover, is an Ottonian ivory of about 1000 telling the story of Christ's first miracle at Cana in three scenes: the Virgin tells Christ and his apostles that the wine has run out; the bridal couple and their guests sit at table; and servants pour water into the stone jars while Christ addresses his mother and the bride. A Gothic goldsmith later set the ivory in a frame of gilded silver and gems.
facts: The museum notes that the reliquary was likely commissioned by Otto the Mild, Duke of Saxony (reigned 1318–48), around 1340.
It was made to contain a leaf from each Gospel and relics of the 11,000 Virgins and other saints, kept in a cavity behind the ivory.
It belongs to the Guelph Treasure, the church treasure of Brunswick Cathedral dispersed in the 20th century.

summary: This small ivory panel, the sliding lid of a box, shows a bearded Christ laying his hand on the eyes of the man born blind, who stands before him with an apostle behind. Its shallow, softly modelled relief belongs to the late antique tradition of Christian ivory carving. The cover was preserved among the relics of the papal chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum in the Lateran.
facts: The Italian museum label describes it as the cover of a medical box (cassetta medica), apt for an image of Christ the healer.
The relics and reliquaries of the Sancta Sanctorum were brought to light in the early 20th century and are now displayed in the Vatican Museums.
notes: Facts come from the Vatican Museums' gallery labels as photographed; no online object record was consulted.

summary: On this worn, oval pectoral of walrus ivory the crucified Christ stands calmly before the cross, his feet on a suppedaneum, while the Hand of God descends from a cloud above; four roundels around him hold the symbols of the Evangelists. A hollow cross-shaped cavity at the back once held a relic, so that the wearer carried both the image and the relic of Christ's Passion close to the heart.
facts: The V&A links the figure style and the Hand of God to late Anglo-Saxon stone roods such as those at Stepney and Romsey.
Such pectoral crosses, worn on a chain or cord, were commonly worn by bishops and abbots.
The cross is only 9 cm high.

summary: This tall silver flask is decorated in relief with standing figures of Christ, the Virgin and two military saints, perhaps Sergios and Bacchos, rendered with the soft, voluminous drapery and large eyes of Byzantine Syria. Its inscription records that Megale and her family gave it in fulfilment of a vow and for the repose of the souls of Heliodorus and Acacius. It probably held consecrated oil for baptism or for anointing the sick and dying.
facts: The Greek inscription reads, in translation: 'For the prayer and salvation of Megale and of her children and nephews, and for the repose of the soul of Heliodorus and Acacius.'
According to the Walters provenance, it was excavated in Syria in 1908–1910 and reached Henry Walters in 1929.
notes: The photograph shows the side with the Virgin; Christ is on another side of the flask, as described by the museum.

summary: A small hollow cross of sheet gold, its rounded arms each marked by three bosses and a pierced cross, holds at its centre a roped medallion of cloisonné enamel: on one side a standing figure of Christ, on the other a bust of Christ, worked in blue, red and green. Worn on the breast, it joined the sign of the cross with the face of the Saviour.
facts: The museum notes that the surfaces are slightly crushed and the lower arm bent, signs of the cross's long use.
It was bought by Henry Walters from the Paris dealer Léon Gruel in 1928.

summary: Around the bowl of this bronze censer runs a frieze of Gospel scenes, identified by the museum as the Annunciation, Nativity, Baptism, Crucifixion and the Women at the Sepulchre, the great feasts of Christ's life from Incarnation to Resurrection. As incense smoke rose through the church, the swinging vessel displayed the whole story of salvation.
facts: Kurt Weitzmann published this piece as 'An East Christian censer' in the Record of the Princeton museum.
It belongs to a group of bronze censers with reliefs of the life of Christ catalogued by Ilse Richter-Siebels in her 1990 study of 'Palestinian' censers.

summary: This small cross-shaped reliquary for a fragment of the True Cross is covered with cloisonné enamel scenes of the childhood of Christ on a translucent green ground: the Annunciation and Visitation in the upper arm, the Nativity with the bathing of the Child at the centre, the journey to Bethlehem and the Adoration of the Magi in the side arms, and the Presentation in the Temple and the Baptism below. It is among the earliest surviving narrative enamels of the Christian world.
facts: The museum label calls it the 'Enamelled Cross of Paschal I'; it was preserved in its own reliquary case among the relics of the Lateran's Sancta Sanctorum chapel.
Whether it was made in Rome or in Byzantium is disputed; the museum label dates it to about the first quarter of the 9th century.
notes: Scene identifications are from the visible enamels and the label's general description ('episodes of the infancy of Christ').

summary: This cross-shaped silver reliquary box, with gilded reliefs on its lid and sides, comes from the treasure of the Sancta Sanctorum. The niello inscription across the lid names Paschal, bishop (pope), and the reliefs show scenes with Christ, among them a haloed Christ standing between attendant figures on the lower arm and an enthroned or seated figure behind an altar at the centre. It is a rare witness to papal patronage of precious metalwork in the age of Charlemagne.
facts: The inscription on the lid includes the name PASCH[ALIS] EPISCOPUS, linking the case to Pope Paschal I (817–824).
Like the enamelled cross of Paschal I, it was preserved among the relics of the papal chapel of the Sancta Sanctorum in the Lateran.
notes: The individual scenes on the case were not verified against a catalogue; the description is limited to what is visible. Scripture omitted for that reason.

summary: A deep sardonyx cup, mounted in gilded silver and strung with pearls, carries around its rim a band of gold cloisonné enamel plaques with busts of Christ, the Virgin and saints; Christ blesses with his right hand and holds a book. The foot bears the name of an emperor Romanos. Like much of the treasury it probably reached Venice after the sack of Constantinople in 1204; it is one of the masterpieces of Byzantine imperial goldsmith work.
facts: The Romanos named on the chalice is usually identified with Romanos I Lekapenos (920–944) or Romanos II (959–963); the Commons description dates the metalwork 959–963.
The stone cup itself may be much older, possibly a reused late Roman hardstone vessel.
Most of the Byzantine hardstone vessels in the Treasury of San Marco arrived as booty from the Fourth Crusade.
notes: The emperor's identity (Romanos I or II) is debated; the date here is given broadly as 10th century.

summary: On a small quatrefoil of gold, about 8 cm high, the crucified Christ hangs on a dark cross beneath the inscription tablet, flanked by the Virgin and Saint John and by two angels above; Greek-letter inscriptions surround the scene. The brilliant colours of the enamel against the gold ground make the image glow like a jewel. It came from the monastery of Shemokmedi in western Georgia, whose treasury preserved many Georgian and Byzantine precious objects.
facts: The Commons record gives its size as 8 × 7.2 cm and describes it as cellular (cloisonné) enamel on a golden ground.
The Shemokmedi treasury, in Guria, also held the Transfiguration icon brought from Zarzma monastery in the 16th century.
notes: Date and attribution follow the Commons file description; I could not consult the museum catalogue.

summary: Christ sits enthroned on a lyre-backed throne, blessing and holding the Gospel book, surrounded by the inscription IHS XPS REX REGNANTIUM, 'Jesus Christ, King of those who rule'. On the other face the senior emperor Romanos I Lekapenos appears with the young Constantine VII, the legitimate Macedonian heir whom he had pushed into second place.
facts: The figure of Christ returned to Byzantine gold coinage after the end of Iconoclasm, and the enthroned type became a standard reverse of the Macedonian period.
Romanos I seized power in 919–920 as father-in-law of the boy emperor Constantine VII, and co-emperors of his own family soon displaced Constantine on the coinage.
notes: Distinct from the Romanos I and Christopher issue already in the collection (cur:objects-coin-romanos-i-christopher-solidus); the museum's date range covers the whole reign.

summary: A pilgrim brought home this wooden box filled with stones gathered at the holy places, several still bearing inscriptions naming where they were collected. Its sliding lid is painted with five scenes: the Nativity and the Baptism at the bottom, the Crucifixion with Christ in a long colobium between the two thieves across the middle, and the Women at the Tomb before the rotunda of the Holy Sepulchre and the Ascension at the top. It is one of the earliest surviving painted cycles of the life of Christ, closely linked to the sites of Jerusalem and its pilgrimage.
facts: The museum label states that the box holds a composition of stones bearing inscriptions of the places where they were collected.
The tomb scene shows the domed rotunda of the Anastasis, the church built over Christ's tomb in Jerusalem.

summary: The Virgin, in a dark red maphorion, holds the Christ Child on her left arm and gestures toward him, while two archangels with staffs stand at her shoulders. The large-eyed, solemn faces are framed by a metal revetment set with medallions. From the monastery of Tsilkani in eastern Georgia, it is one of the oldest icons of the Georgian Church.
facts: Tsilkani is an early Christian monastery in the historic region of Kartli in eastern Georgia.
Commons gives the date as 9th century; the icon is now kept in the Art Museum of Georgia in Tbilisi.
notes: The dating of the painted panel and of its revetment is debated; some scholars place the painting earlier. Medium given in general terms.

summary: The larger of the two great Mercian crosses at Sandbach is carved on its east face with a stacked sequence of Gospel scenes in small panels. Sources describe the Adoration of the Magi at the top, then the Crucifixion with the four Evangelist symbols around the cross, the Nativity below it, and further down the Transfiguration and Christ between Saints Peter and Paul. Though weathered, the panels form one of the richest cycles of Christ's life in Anglo-Saxon sculpture.
facts: The most recent dating places the larger cross in the early 9th century and the smaller around the middle of that century.
Broken up after the Reformation or during the Civil War, the crosses were reassembled under the Cheshire historian George Ormerod in 1816.
They are a Grade I listed building and scheduled monument.

links.label: English Heritage: history of the Sandbach Crosses

notes: Scene sequence follows the UCC Text and Image database and Britain Express; English Heritage describes the scenes more loosely. The photograph shows the upper part of the east face.

summary: This rare free-standing cross from eastern Scotland is carved on every face. The face shown is usually interpreted as Christ flanked by angels at the head of the cross, above the four Evangelists on the shaft; on the badly weathered opposite face the antiquary Alexander Gordon recorded a Crucifixion in 1726. Its sculpture shows Irish influence and belongs to the last phase of Pictish carving.
facts: The Camus Cross and the Dupplin Cross are the only intact free-standing crosses of this period in eastern Scotland.
Local tradition held that it marked the grave of 'Camus', a Norse leader supposedly defeated by Malcolm II; the name more likely comes from the vanished village of Camuston.
Robert Maule, its earliest describer, read the main figure scene as Moses giving out the Law.
notes: The photograph appears to show the east face (Christ with angels and Evangelists); the Crucifixion face is largely weathered away.

summary: The figurative east face of this perfectly preserved Celtic cross shows, on the shaft just below the head, the Virgin enthroned with the Christ Child, flanked by angels; on the arms appear Cain slaying Abel and the Sacrifice of Isaac, with David killing the lion above the central boss. The Virgin and Child closely recalls those on the Iona crosses and folio 7v of the Book of Kells.
facts: It is often considered the finest surviving Celtic cross in Scotland and was carved from a single block.
The Virgin-and-Child type may echo the Roman Maria Regina imagery of the iconoclast period.
The west face is largely abstract, with snake-and-boss roundels and four lions around the central boss.

summary: The weathered head of the Donaghmore cross carries the Crucifixion at its centre, the outstretched arms of Christ spanning the ring. The shaft below holds a sequence of biblical panels, including an Adoration of the Magi with the Virgin and the Christ Child on her lap. Composed of parts of two different crosses, it is a characteristic scripture cross of the Ulster group.
facts: The cross is a composite: its shaft and head come from two different crosses.
A replica was erected in the graveyard behind it in 2001.
notes: Date is tentative in all sources consulted ('possibly 10th century').

summary: The North Cross at Monasterboice preserves its ringed head, whose west face shows a simplified Crucifixion: Christ with arms outstretched, flanked by the spear-bearer and the sponge-bearer. The rest of the face is filled with spirals, and the volutes sit unusually on the ring rather than at the crossing.
facts: Only the head and a short section of the upper shaft are original; the cross now stands on a replacement shaft about 3 metres high.
Monasterboice also preserves Muiredach's Cross and the West Cross, both already in the collection.

summary: The shaft of the west cross at Old Kilcullen stands without its head among the ruins of an early monastery. On its west face, according to Peter Harbison's reading, the panels show from top to bottom a horseman, Samson slaying the lion, and Christ entering Jerusalem. The simplified relief is typical of the granite crosses of the Barrow valley.
facts: The panel identifications follow Peter Harbison's corpus of Irish high crosses, as cited in the photograph's description.
notes: The Entry into Jerusalem panel is small and weathered in the photograph; identification relies on Harbison. Material (granite) is assumed from the regional group and should be checked.

summary: The Crucifixion fills the centre of the head on the east face of the North Cross at Castledermot, surrounded by the twelve apostles in rows on the arms and shaft. Lower down, a raven brings bread to the desert hermits Paul and Anthony, a monastic image of the Eucharist, above a spiral-carved base.
facts: The other face of the same cross carries a musician playing a lyre (cruit), one of the best-known images of an early Irish instrument.
notes: Scene identifications from the photographer's detailed Commons description (A. F. Borchert).

summary: At the centre of the west face of the South Cross the crucified Christ is flanked by David playing the harp and the Sacrifice of Isaac, the Old Testament type of his offering. Below, the shaft shows the hermits Paul and Anthony fed by the raven, Adam and Eve, the Temptation of Saint Anthony and Daniel in the lions' den, and a hunting scene on the base.
facts: The pairing of the Crucifixion with the Sacrifice of Isaac expresses the early Christian reading of Isaac as a figure of Christ.
notes: Scene identifications from the photographer's Commons description.

summary: On this carved block two winged angels, their robes rendered in parallel grooves, fly toward a central frontal bust with large almond eyes, long hair and a beard, holding a fold of drapery. The church of Santa María de Lara is celebrated for containing what is often called the earliest image of Christ in Spanish art, and this block is commonly associated with that identification. Its flat, linear style is one of the most distinctive voices of Visigothic sculpture.
facts: The church is generally dated to the late 7th or early 8th century, though some scholars have placed it as late as the 10th century.
It was declared a national monument on 25 November 1929, after being rediscovered by a local priest in 1921.
Two other reliefs, depicting Evangelists, were stolen in 2004 and recovered in a British garden in 2019 by the Dutch art detective Arthur Brand.

links.label: Wikipedia: Hermitage of Santa María de Lara

notes: Sources disagree on which block depicts Christ: some locate the Christ bust above the keystone of the arch, others among the loose blocks inside; a second loose block shows a beardless bust holding a cross between angels. The identification of this bearded bust as Christ could not be confirmed from a scholarly catalogue.
